primary_text_source: Full acting text (Dramatists Play Service ed.) via archive.org item 'an-inspector-calls-full-text'; cross-checked against LitCharts and GradeSaver. Wording differences known to be edition-specific (e.g. 'twenty-two and six', 'a chap easily turns nasty', 'cheap labour - they're people') were NOT flagged.

findings.claim: All 48 practice questions are labelled '40 marks - Post-1914 Essay' but every mark ladder runs Top band (21-25) / Upper-mid (16-20) / Mid (11-15) / Lower-mid (6-10) / Lower band (1-5).
findings.truth: The Edexcel post-1914 British play or novel essay is 40 marks: AO1 16 + AO3 16 + AO4 8. A ladder topping at 25 tells students a perfect answer scores 25. Rescaled to fifths of 40: 33-40 / 25-32 / 17-24 / 9-16 / 1-8, and the bottom band renamed to the house label 'Low band'.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md, 'Breakdown of Assessment Objectives by component': Questions 7 to 30 = AO1 16, AO3 16, AO4 8, total 40.

findings.claim: 'an essay response worth up to 40 marks (including 4 for SPaG)'
findings.truth: AO4 (spelling, punctuation and grammar) is worth 8 marks on this question, not 4. The 4-mark SPaG figure is the AQA modern-text pattern, not Edexcel.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md AO breakdown table: Questions 7 to 30, AO4 = 8; AO4 = 5% of the qualification (8 of 160 raw marks).

findings.claim: AO4 'includes using literary terminology correctly (dramatic irony, stage directions, symbolism, tricolon, etc.)'. Repeated in the exam tip ('accurate use of literary terminology (AO4)'), in knowledge_checks[4].right[2] ('Spelling, punctuation, grammar, and use of specialist terminology') and in flashcard_questions[4].
findings.truth: AO4 is 'Use a range of vocabulary and sentence structures for clarity, purpose and effect, with accurate spelling and punctuation'. Subject terminology sits under AO2, which is NOT assessed on this question at all. A student who spends the AO4 effort on terminology instead of accuracy loses marks.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md, Assessment Objectives table (AO4 wording) and the component breakdown (Questions 7 to 30 assess AO1, AO3 and AO4 only).

findings.claim: 'For AO4 (SPaG), use literary terminology precisely and structure your paragraphs with a clear argument.'
findings.truth: Same error as F3. Paragraph structure and argument are AO1; terminology is AO2. AO4 rewards accurate written English only.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md, AO4 definition.

findings.claim: 'I'm ashamed of you as well - yes both of you' is attributed to Sheila in nine places: L5 content (x2), L5 knowledge_checks[2], L5 flashcard[7], L5 practice[1] and [3] (stimulus + mark scheme), L3 practice[4] (stimulus + mark scheme), L3 flashcard[13], L7 flashcard[13], L8 content quotation bank and L8 practice[2] mark scheme.
findings.truth: The line is ERIC's, in Act 3. MRS BIRLING: 'I should think not. Eric, I'm absolutely ashamed of you.' ERIC: 'Well, I don't blame you. But don't forget I'm ashamed of you as well - yes, both of you.' L3 compounded the error by setting it as the stimulus for a question about Acts 1 and 2.
findings.evidence: Full text, Act 3: MRS. BIRLING '...Eric, I'm absolutely ashamed of you.' / ERIC 'Well, I don't blame you. But don't forget I'm ashamed of you as well-yes, both of you.'

findings.claim: 'He is horrified when he learns that his mother turned Eva away from the charity: "You're not the kind of father a chap could go to when he's in trouble."'
findings.truth: Eric says this to his FATHER, and it comes before the charity revelation. Birling has just said 'You damned fool - why didn't you come to me when you found yourself in this mess?' about the stolen money. Eric's reaction to his mother is the separate 'Then - you killed her' speech.
findings.evidence: Full text, Act 3: BIRLING '...why didn't you come to me when you found yourself in this mess?' / ERIC 'Because you're not the kind of father a chap could go to when he's in trouble - that's why.'

findings.claim: 'Gerald telephones the local police and discovers that there is no Inspector Goole on the force.'
findings.truth: Gerald met a police sergeant he knows in the street; Birling then telephoned the chief constable, Colonel Roberts. Gerald made the later call to the Infirmary. Lesson 6 describes the same events correctly.
findings.evidence: Full text, Act 3: GERALD 'I met a police sergeant I know down the road...' / BIRLING 'Ring up the Chief Constable - Colonel Roberts.' / GERALD (to Infirmary) 'Brumley eight-nine-eight-six...'

findings.claim: 'Gerald insists his feelings were genuine: "I didn't feel about her as she felt about me."'
findings.truth: The quotation says the opposite of the claim. It is Gerald's hesitant answer to Sheila's question 'Were you in love with her?' - an admission that his feelings were weaker than hers. A student following this framing would misread the line.
findings.evidence: Full text, Act 2: SHEILA 'Were you in love with her, Gerald?' / GERALD (hesitatingly) 'It's hard to say. I didn't feel about her the way she felt about me.'

findings.claim: Sheila: 'I respect you more than I've ever done before - because at least you're being honest.' (also flashcard_questions[3])
findings.truth: A splice of two separate Act 2 lines. The real wording is 'I don't dislike you as I did half an hour ago, Gerald. In fact, in some odd way, I rather respect you more than I've ever done before' followed later by 'And now at least you've been honest.' The joined version is not a quotation from the play.
findings.evidence: Full text, Act 2; also LitCharts quotes page, https://www.litcharts.com/lit/an-inspector-calls/quotes

findings.claim: 'His family, the Crofts, are "an old country family - landed people"' (also knowledge_checks[3] and flashcard_questions[8]).
findings.truth: The play says 'an old COUNTY family - landed people and so forth', and it is Birling describing Lady Croft, Gerald's mother, when explaining why she thinks Gerald could have married better socially. 'County family' means long-established landed gentry of a county; 'country family' is a misremembering and would be marked as an inaccurate quotation.
findings.evidence: Full text, Act 1: BIRLING '...Don't blame her. She comes from an old county family-landed people and so forth-and so it's only natural.'

findings.claim: Sheila: 'You gave yourself away as soon as he mentioned her name.'
findings.truth: The play reads 'her other name' - the point is that Daisy Renton is Eva's second name.
findings.evidence: Full text, Act 1: SHEILA 'Oh, don't be stupid. We haven't much time. You gave yourself away as soon as he mentioned her other name.'

findings.claim: 'Birling sacked Eva, Sheila got her sacked again, Gerald used and abandoned her, Mrs Birling denied her charity, and Eric got her pregnant.' The key fact and its revision tip ask students to list the five links 'in order'.
findings.truth: That is the order of the Inspector's interrogation, not the chain of events. Eva was already pregnant by Eric when she went to the committee - that is why Mrs Birling's refusal is the last link before the suicide, and why Eric can tell his mother 'she came to you to protect me'. Reordered to Eric then Mrs Birling.
findings.evidence: Full text, Act 3: Eric gave Eva about fifty pounds of stolen money, she refused to take more, and then applied to the committee; ERIC to MRS BIRLING 'Then - you killed her.'

findings.claim: flashcard[7] asks 'What Assessment Objective best describes Priestley's purpose in the play?' and answers 'A political argument that class and patriarchy combine to harm working-class women.'
findings.truth: An assessment objective is a marking criterion, not a writer's purpose. The card as written teaches a false idea of what an AO is. The answer is a sound thematic point, so the question was rewritten to match it.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md, Assessment Objectives table.

findings.claim: '(Gerald did cry when describing his affair)', repeated in practice_questions[1] as 'He cries during his confession'.
findings.truth: The text gives Gerald the stage direction '(distressed)' and has him ask to be alone. He is never shown crying. Sheila is the character who cries.
findings.evidence: Full text, Act 2, Gerald's exit; the crying stage directions in Acts 2 and 3 belong to Sheila.

findings.claim: 'Eva "was very grateful" and "intensely grateful"'
findings.truth: Only 'intensely grateful' is in the play. 'Very grateful' is presented in quotation marks but does not appear; the doubled quotation is redundant as well as unattested.
findings.evidence: Full text, Act 2: GERALD 'She was young and pretty and warm-hearted-and intensely grateful. I became at once the most important person in her life.'

findings.claim: 'In the Edexcel English Literature exam (Component 1, Section B), context is assessed through AO3.'
findings.truth: 'Component 1' is on the house banned-string list, so the whole unit would fail validation. Reworded to name the question instead, and the real AO3 weighting (16 of 40) added.
findings.evidence: scripts/_retrofc/CHECK_PROMPT.md banned strings; spec AO breakdown.

findings.claim: Sheila: 'It doesn't make any difference ... You began to learn something. And now you've stopped.' (L4 content, L4 practice[3], L4 flashcard[10], L4 knowledge_checks[4].right[2], L7 content, L7 practice)
findings.truth: Both halves are Sheila's and both are Act 3, but they are separate moments and the first drops a word: 'All right. But it doesn't make any real difference, y'know.' The second half is verbatim. No marks are at stake in a closed-book exam, and correcting it would touch six places, so it is recorded rather than edited.
findings.evidence: Full text, Act 3: SHEILA 'All right. But it doesn't make any real difference, y'know.' and SHEILA 'I tell you - whoever that Inspector was, it was anything but a joke. You knew it then. You began to learn something. And now you've stopped. You're ready to go on in the same old way.'

findings.claim: practice_questions[5] is 'Write a practice PEEAL paragraph analysing the significance of the stage direction...' but carries the type label '40 marks - Post-1914 Essay' and a full five-band mark ladder.
findings.truth: It is a revision exercise, not a board question - a single paragraph cannot be worth 40 marks. Two defensible fixes: (a) relabel the type to a non-exam label such as 'Exam skill - PEEAL paragraph' and drop the band ladder, or (b) rewrite the task as a full essay question on Priestley's use of stage directions. Recommend (b), because the mark ladder and the stimulus-plus-essay format are then honest and the content of the model answer survives. Left as a 40-mark item for now, with the ladder rescaled like the rest. ORCHESTRATOR: left as NOTE - rewriting a question is authoring, not a surgical fix; logged for the question-type relabel workstream.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md: the post-1914 section is one essay question from a choice of two.

findings.claim: knowledge_checks[4].right[2] describes Sheila as 'the only character who fully transforms from privilege to conscience'.
findings.truth: The same lesson argues at length that Eric also accepts full responsibility and is transformed. 'The most complete transformation' (the wording used in knowledge_checks[0]) is accurate; 'the only character' contradicts the lesson body. Not edited because the match answer itself is still right.
findings.evidence: L5 content_html, 'Eric Birling: The Damaged Product' and 'Eric and Sheila: The Younger Generation Compared'.

findings.claim: Bare 'Section B' appears in the exam tips of lessons 1, 3, 6 and 7 and in the description of lesson 8.
findings.truth: The house banned list targets 'Paper 1 Section B'-style codes. Bare 'Section B' is borderline. Only the instance carrying 'Component 1' (F16) and the one in lesson 8's conclusion were reworded. If the validator rejects bare 'Section B' too, five more strings need the same treatment.
findings.evidence: scripts/_retrofc/CHECK_PROMPT.md banned strings.

summary: No lesson was clean: every one of the 48 practice questions labelled a 40-mark post-1914 essay carried a mark ladder that stopped at 25 (F1). The other serious faults are exam-claim errors in the technique lesson - AO4 called 4 marks instead of 8 and described as rewarding literary terminology (F2-F4) - and a quotation misattributed across four lessons: 'I'm ashamed of you as well - yes both of you' is Eric's Act 3 line, not Sheila's (F5). Six further findings correct plot framing and quotation wording verified against the full text.
